Tweedie outcomes checked with a Gaussian model

A model can reproduce correlation but miss other features

These simulated Tweedie outcomes are nonnegative and skewed, with some zeros and different variability for women and men. We deliberately fit an exchangeable Gaussian model: the same effects and variance for both roles. Its shared dyad intercept allows positive partner correlation; there is no member-difference random effect, but observation-level variance is still estimated.

Every code chunk below runs when this document is rendered. Each check is followed by all the complete panels it produces, in their original order.

Fit the model and simulate once

Run from dev/diagnostic_checks/ to read the saved dataset of 120 female-male dyads. All checks reuse the same 2,000 simulated datasets.

library(dyadMLM)
tweedie_data <- read.csv(
  "distribution-diagnostics/results/tweedie-gaussian/data.csv",
  colClasses = c(role = "factor")
)
tweedie_data$dyad <- factor(tweedie_data$dyad)
gaussian_model <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(
  outcome ~ predictor + (1 | dyad),
  family = gaussian(), dispformula = ~1, data = tweedie_data
)
gaussian_simulations <- simulate_dyad_responses(
  gaussian_model, nsim = 2000, seed = 100105
)

Supply the fitting data because role is absent from the model frame. Roles split the plots without changing the fitted model’s assumptions.

Check residuals

Start with everyone together. The first page checks the residual distribution; the second checks patterns across predicted outcomes.

check_residuals(gaussian_simulations, role = NULL, seed = 123, ask = FALSE)

Now separate women and men using the same simulations. predictors adds a page showing how residuals change with the predictor. This call produces three pages.

check_residuals(
  gaussian_simulations, dyad = dyad, role = role, data = tweedie_data,
  predictors = "predictor",
  seed = 123, ask = FALSE
)

The QQ curves and 10-bin PIT histogram show the same distribution mismatch in two ways. The outlier row compares counts beyond the finite simulated response range. Predicted outcome means the model prediction with random effects set to zero. The separate predictor page uses the supplied predictor values. Judge the red quartiles against their matching blue bands; the horizontal lines at 0.25, 0.50 and 0.75 are guides.

Check outcomes

check_zeros = TRUE includes zero counts. The call produces one complete panel: the raw outcome distribution, SDs and largest deviations after subtracting predictions, and zero counts.

check_outcomes(
  gaussian_simulations, dyad = dyad, role = role, data = tweedie_data,
  check_zeros = TRUE, ask = FALSE
)

The Gaussian model generates negative values, misses the male zeros, and understates the largest deviations from predictions. Its common SD is too large for female responses and too small for male responses.

Check partner dependence

The default check subtracts the same predictions from observed and simulated outcomes. It produces one complete panel for this composition.

check_partner_dependence(
  gaussian_simulations, dyad = dyad, role = role,
  data = tweedie_data, ask = FALSE
)

Here the role SDs repeat the outcome check. The mean–difference correlation also reveals unequal variability, while the partner correlation agrees reasonably well. Omitting the difference random effect does not by itself force a mismatch: the shared intercept and observation-level noise can reproduce positive partner correlation.

For comparison, request the same panel for raw outcomes:

check_partner_dependence(
  gaussian_simulations, dyad = dyad, role = role, data = tweedie_data,
  response = "raw", ask = FALSE
)

This includes variation explained by the predictor; the role-variance mismatch remains visible. Several assumptions are wrong here, so a failed check does not identify a single cause. Residual curve envelopes cover each panel jointly; scalar ranges describe individual comparisons. Coverage is not simultaneous across all plots. Fitted parameters stay fixed, so these are descriptive checks, not significance tests.
